newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean legislators defend U.S. eco-millionaire.
newsitem.headline: Chilean legislators defend U.S. eco-millionaire.

text.p: Three Chilean congressmen asked the government on Friday to stop what they called the persecution of U.S. millionaire Douglas Tompkins, who is trying to create a vast nature reserve in southern Chile.
The lawmakers accused officials in President Eduardo Frei's government of harassing Tompkins to satisfy nationalist groups and the interests of timber and salmon-farming firms.

"Tompkins' opponents are trying to stop him by inventing fantasies. First they said he wanted to create a Jewish state, then that he supported abortion, then that he was a spy," said deputy Guido Girardi of the centre-left Party for Democracy.
"What you have is a smear campaign, but after two years investigating every aspect of Douglas Tompkins, every argument against him has proved groundless," he said.

The three lawmakers told a news conference that concerns that Tompkins' project was a threat to national security because it stretched from the Pacific coast to the Argentine border were also groundless.

"There are people who want us to believe that one man can put all our national security into jeopardy because he buys some land and wants to preserve it. They would have to think the Chilean people ignorant to believe that," said Arturo Longton, deputy for the centre-right party National Renewal.

Tompkins, a California clothing magnate, bought up an area of virgin forest in southern Chile the size of Rhode Island and says he will donate it to a Chilean ecology foundation on the condition it be preserved and opened to the public.

He has met strong opposition from much of Frei's government, the military and businessmen who think he is bankrolling Chile's growing environmental movement, which they see as an obstacle for the country's economic development.
Chile's news media has also turned against the American, and one television station suggested he was a CIA spy.

Girardi said the government was divided on how to handle Tompkins, with Frei's chief political adviser Juan Villarzu and Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos supporting him, and Deputy Interior Minister Belisario Velasco strongly opposed.

"There are some officials who have no interest in the environment and are persecuting this man, but it's not the position of the whole government," said Girardi, whose party is one of four in Frei's coalition government.

Tompkins charged this week that he was being harassed. His lawyer said the harassment campaign included death threats, phone taps and air force planes buzzing his home in a remote valley. The government has denied Tompkins' charges.
